findings.title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER computes encodings and discards them
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write r and s into them, and throw the results away. This is dead code that does redundant BigInteger encoding work on every signature conversion and suggests the encoding logic was not carefully reviewed.

findings.title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER builds r and s with a forced leading zero byte, producing non-minimal and wrong integers
findings.body: The method copies each half of the signature into an array of length len+1 with a leading 0 byte, then calls new BigInteger(r). That is always non-negative, which is correct for the sign, but the DER encoding then writes BigInteger.toByteArray() of the value, which is minimal. The only real issue is that signLength/2 is assumed equal to each component length; for odd or mismatched signLength inputs the arraycopy silently misbehaves or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBounds instead of an IOException. Also the method is not used by the ECDSA verification path in the test, so the round-trip test covers only the happy path.

findings.title: readInteger drops the sign-extension semantics needed for ECDSA components and does not check length
findings.body: readInteger reads the content with read(length) and builds BigInteger(bytes) without validating that length is positive or that the value is non-negative. ECDSA r/s values from a malicious or malformed DER signature can be arbitrarily large or negative; integerToBytes then truncates them silently, so a signature with out-of-range components can be mapped to a different valid-looking concatenated value instead of being rejected.

findings.title: readSequence loop can run forever or misparse when element length is zero
findings.body: In readSequence the loop subtracts bytes.length from the remaining length; readNext returns the full TLV including tag and length. If the decoder returns indefinite length (-1 from readLength) or a zero-length element, length never reaches zero and the loop can spin or read past the sequence. Indefinite length is not rejected here.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the provider of a default KeyStore instance
findings.body: The method creates a KeyStore of the default type and returns its Provider, which is not a BouncyCastle provider and is only the provider of an uninitialized keystore. Callers that expect BC (e.g. for registering or looking up BC algorithms) will get an unrelated provider, or the method may throw IllegalStateException on a misconfigured keystore type.

findings.title: Provider order 100 ranks below DefaultCryptoProvider but most methods throw UnsupportedOperationException
findings.body: CryptoIntegration now picks the highest order. This provider has order 100 while Default/Elytron/FIPS use 200, so it is chosen only when they are absent. But if it is selected (authz-client used standalone), every method other than getEcdsaCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException, including getKeyStore's siblings and createECParams, so any non-ECDSA path in the client fails at runtime.

findings.title: Multiple providers no longer rejected, changing detection semantics silently
findings.body: Previously multiple CryptoProvider implementations on the classpath caused an IllegalStateException. Now the highest-order one is silently chosen and the rest only logged at debug level. A misconfigured deployment with two providers of equal order gets an arbitrary pick (sort is stable but ServiceLoader order is not deterministic across classpaths) with no warning.

findings.title: Ignored providers logged via debugf with non-constant format string
findings.body: logger.debugf(builder.toString()) passes the built string as a format pattern; any '%' in a class name or future text will be misinterpreted as a format specifier and throw or garble the message. Use debugf with a format argument.

findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks all existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default. Any third-party or other in-repo CryptoProvider implementation that does not override it will fail to compile. Providing a default would preserve compatibility.

findings.title: Test only checks round trip of concatenated RS, not that DER is valid or matches the reference
findings.body: The test asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) equals x, but never verifies the produced DER against the original signature or checks signature verification succeeds. A symmetric bug in both directions would pass. It should verify the signature with the converted DER and cover edge cases such as leading-zero/high-bit components.
